title: Instruction Sequence and Control Flow
definition: An instruction sequence is an ordered representation whose next executed instruction is determined by the execution model and explicit control-flow rules.
purpose: Support step-by-step prediction while preventing the false belief that textual order can never change.
history: Stored-program machines use ordered instructions and control transfers; modern systems add optimization while preserving architectural behavior.
mental_model: A cursor identifies the next rule; ordinary steps advance it, while control instructions select another valid location.
analogy: A choose-your-path procedure models control transfer; it fails to represent parallel and speculative hardware details.
relationships: is interpreted by an execution model
real_world_usage: Tracing a debugger one step at a time
common_mistakes: Confusing architectural order with physical micro-operation timing
industry_notes: Debuggers present a sequential abstraction even when runtimes and processors optimize internal execution.
ai_notes: Require AI-generated traces to identify the next-instruction rule at every step.
interview_notes: Ask the candidate to predict a trace containing one branch and explain skipped instructions.
exercise_candidates: Trace a sequence with one conditional control transfer
lab_candidates: Execute a tiny instruction table and record each cursor movement
project_candidates: Implement and test the instruction pointer of the simulator
